DECISION AND OPINION ON REVIEW 
Timely Petition for Review having been filed by the Petitioner herein and notice given to 
all parties, the Commission, after considering the issues of causal connection, occupational 
disease, permanent partial disability, legal error, evidentiary error, and Section 1(d) - Section 1(f), 
and being advised of the facts and law, affirms and adopts the Decision of the Arbitrator, which is 
attached hereto and made a part hereof.   
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Decision of the 
Arbitrator filed October 1, 2025 is hereby affirmed and adopted. 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Respondent pay to 
Petitioner interest under §19(n) of the Act, if any. 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Respondent shall have 
credit for all amounts paid, if any, to or on behalf of the Petitioner on account of said accidental 
injury. 
 Based upon the denial of compensation herein, no bond is set by the Commission. The 
party commencing the proceedings for review in the Circuit Court shall file with the Commission 
a Notice of Intent to File for Review in Circuit Court.

ILLINOIS WORKERS’ COMPENSATION COMMISSION 
 
ARBITRATION DECISION 
 
 
JOHN MARTIN  
Case # 22 WC 033516 
Employee/Petitioner 
 
v. 
 
 
ICG ILLINOIS, LLC 
Employer/Respondent 
 
 
An Application for Adjustment of Claim was filed in this matter, and a Notice of Hearing was mailed to each 
party.  The matter was heard by the Honorable Adam Hinrichs, Arbitrator of the Commission, in the city of 
Springfield, on July 29, 2025.  After reviewing all of the evidence presented, the Arbitrator hereby makes 
findings on the disputed issues checked below and attaches those findings to this document.  
 
DISPUTED ISSUES 
 
 
A. 
 Was Respondent operating under and subject to the Illinois Workers' Compensation or Occupational  
 
Diseases Act? 
B. 
 Was there an employee-employer relationship? 
C. 
 Did an accident occur that arose out of and in the course of Petitioner's employment by Respondent? 
D. 
 What was the date of the accident? 
E. 
 Was timely notice of the accident given to Respondent? 
F. 
 Is Petitioner's current condition of ill-being causally related to the injury? 
G. 
 What were Petitioner's earnings? 
H. 
 What was Petitioner's age at the time of the accident? 
I. 
 What was Petitioner's marital status at the time of the accident? 
J.

 paid all appropriate charges for all reasonable and necessary medical services? 
K. 
 What temporary benefits are in dispute?   
 
 
 TPD

 What is the nature and extent of the injury?  
M. 
 Should penalties or fees be imposed upon Respondent? 
N. 
 Is Respondent due any credit? 
O. 
 Other  Sections 1(d)-(f) of the Occupational Diseases Act

FINDINGS 
 
On June 1, 2021, Respondent was operating under and subject to the provisions of the Act.   
 
On this date, an employee-employer relationship did exist between Petitioner and Respondent.   
 
On this date, Petitioner did not sustain an accident that arose out of and in the course of employment. 
 
Timely notice of this accident was given to Respondent. 
 
Petitioner's current condition of ill-being is not causally related to the accident. 
 
In the year preceding the injury, Petitioner’s earnings were   $59,525.99 and the average weekly wage was 
$1,144.73. 
 
On the date of accident, Petitioner was 60 years of age, married with 0 dependent children. 
 
Petitioner claims no medical. 
 
Respondent shall be given a credit of $0 for TTD, $0 for TPD, $0 for maintenance, and $0 for other benefits, for 
a total credit of $0. 
 
Respondent is entitled to a credit of $0 under Section 8(j) of the Act. 
 
ORDER 
 
Petitioner has failed to prove an injury/disease under the Occupational Diseases Act by a preponderance of the 
evidence.  
 
Petitioner’s request for benefits under the Occupational Diseases Act is denied.  
 
RULES REGARDING APPEALS: Unless a party files a Petition for Review within 30 days after receipt of this 
decision, and perfects a review in accordance with the Act and Rules, then this decision shall be entered as the 
decision of the Commission.   
 
STATEMENT OF INTEREST RATE: If the Commission reviews this award, interest at the rate set forth on the Notice 
of Decision of Arbitrator shall accrue from the date listed below to the day before the date of payment; 
however, if an employee's appeal results in either no change or a decrease in this award, interest shall not 
accrue.   
 
 
 
Signature of Arbitrator 
 
 
 
                                                                                                                                                      OCTOBER 1 2025 
26IWCC0133

 
3
 
FINDINGS OF FACT 
 
Petitioner testified to a work history in the mines stating he performed belt moves, power moves, room moves, 
ran a ram car, roof bolted, dusted a lot, and hauled dust. He was on the track for about the last two years hauling 
supplies and dust. He testified that he started working in the coal mines in the 1980s and he ended his career 
about four to five years prior to arbitration. During his time in the mines, Petitioner testified that he noticed a 
cough. He additionally testified that his body is worn out. He testified he cannot function like he used to in 
reference to breathing. He testified that he has trouble mowing the yard and he has to sit down for 20 to 25 
minutes. He testified that he walks his dog because the dog has to lose weight, and he can hardly do that 
anymore. 
 
Petitioner testified he has been a smoker for probably 30 years. He testified that when he worked at the coal 
mines he didn't smoke that much because he could not smoke in the mine and estimated his smoking at half a 
pack a day. He testified that while working in the mines he worked an average of 10 hours a day, five days a 
week, sometimes six days. Petitioner testified that he probably began smoking around 15 or 16 years old, and he 
was still smoking at the time of arbitration. He stated that at some point he quit smoking for around three years. 
He stated that his employment ended with the mine when he was laid off about four years prior to arbitration.  
 
Petitioner testified that he did not continuously work as a coal miner from the 1980’s through the time he was 
laid off in 2021. He testified he worked at Bridgestone/Firestone in Decatur for six years. Petitioner has not 
worked anywhere since he left the mine. Petitioner testified that he never underwent NIOSH chest x-ray 
screenings. He testified that his primary care physicians are with Springfield Memorial Health and Springfield 
Clinic and that he was always honest with his providers as to the problems he did or did not have when he was 
being seen. Petitioner testified that he saw Dr. Suhail Istanbouly one time at his attorney's request as part of this 
claim. 
 
Petitioner testified that he does not take any medications for his breathing. He testified that he spends his days 
now just mowing his grass and walking the dog. He testified he mows with a riding and push mower and mows 
the area the size of two lots around his home. He also testified that he goes camping in a pull behind camper. He 
testified that he has gone camping about five times so far this year. He testified that he and his wife used to 
travel, but she has returned to work. 
 
Dr. Suhail Istanbouly Testimony 
 
Dr. Istanbouly is board certified in internal medicine, pulmonary medicine, critical care medicine and sleep 
medicine. He testified that in April of 2019 he moved his practice to the Chicago area. (PX 1, p. 5). He testified 
that he began working in Southern Illinois in 2003 as a pulmonologist and critical care specialist. He opened his 
own practice in 2008 where he did inpatient and outpatient care in his specialties which are pulmonary, critical 
care, and sleep medicine. (PX 1, pp. 5-6).  
 
Dr. Istanbouly testified that he does black lung examinations and writes reports on coal miners at the request of 
their attorneys. He testified that when he gives an examination, he reads the x-ray, takes the pulmonary function 
testing, and patient history himself. He testified that he performs such examinations for the Department of 
Labor. (PX 1, p. 7). He testified that he was removed from the approved list to perform Department of Labor 
exams for black lung due to paperwork issues after he left the area in 2019. (PX 1, pp. 49-50). He testified that 
in Chicago, he practices at Hines VA Hospital in pulmonary and sleep medicine. He testified that he comes to 
Southern Illinois once a month and he has a satellite clinic in Marshall Browning Hospital in DuQuoin, where 
he sees pulmonary and sleep medicine cases. He testified he still performs black lung examinations in Southern 
Illinois. (PX 1, p. 7). 
26IWCC0133

 
4
 
Dr. Istanbouly testified that he examined Petitioner at the request of his attorney on January 24, 2023, and he 
authored a report following the examination. (PX 1, p. 8). Dr. Istanbouly testified that Petitioner was 62 years 
old at the time of his examination and had 32 years of coal mining, all underground. (PX1, p. 10). He indicated 
in his history that Petitioner worked five to six days a week, 10 hours each shift. (Petitioner’s Exhibit No. 1, pp. 
10-11). 
 
Dr. Istanbouly testified that Petitioner currently smoked half a pack a day and had a 40-pack-year history of 
smoking. He testified that Petitioner has had a daily cough for 10 years that was productive of three tablespoons 
of sputum a day, and it was aggravated by laughing and strenuous activity. He testified that the Petitioner 
occasionally wheezes. He testified that the Petitioner believed that his physical capacity is declining slowly. 
(PX 1, p. 12). Dr. Istanbouly testified that the spirometry that he took of Petitioner was within the range of 
normal. Dr. Istanbouly diagnosed simple coal workers’ pneumoconiosis and chronic bronchitis. (PX 1, pp. 13-
14). 
 
Dr. Istanbouly testified that looking at the totality of Petitioner's dataset, knowing that COPD comes in two 
forms, emphysema or chronic bronchitis, there is a big deal of overlap between the two entities. He testified that 
when he labels someone with chronic bronchitis, he cannot rule out the possibility of emphysema completely. 
He testified that in Petitioner's case, his clinical presentation is more consistent with chronic bronchitis rather 
than emphysema, but he cannot rule out emphysema for sure. Dr. Istanbouly testified that if he has a chest CT 
scan showing emphysematous changes, the diagnosis of emphysema is confirmed. He testified that a finding on 
CT scan of fibrosis is consistent with coal workers’ pneumoconiosis. He testified that a person can have fibrosis 
in his lungs that is apparent on radiographic studies that has multiple causes. (PX 1, pp. 14-15).  
 
Dr. Istanbouly testified that a person can have normal spirometry and still have a significantly reduced DLCO. 
He also testified within a reasonable degree of medical certainty based on Petitioner's occupational history, x-
ray findings, and symptoms that Petitioner has coal workers’ pneumoconiosis related to his coal mine 
employment. He testified that based on all the data he has, within a reasonable degree of medical certainty, 
Petitioner has chronic bronchitis, which is a form of COPD, caused by coal dust inhalation and smoking. He 
testified that if the CT scan showed emphysematous changes, Petitioner has emphysema, and it would be related 
to both long-term coal dust inhalation and smoking. (PX 1, pp. 16-18). Dr. Istanbouly testified that Petitioner 
has clinically significant pulmonary impairment in terms of signs and symptoms of pulmonary disease. He 
testified that Petitioner has radiographically apparent pulmonary impairment in the form of abnormalities in the 
structure of his lungs that would result in damaged tissue so that the tissue could not perform the usual function 
of normal healthy lung tissue. Dr. Istanbouly testified that if Petitioner has a reduced DLCO then he has 
pulmonary impairment. (PX 1, pp. 18-19).  
 
Dr. Istanbouly testified it is advisable for Petitioner from a medical standpoint to avoid any further coal dust 
inhalation and smoking to prevent the progression of his pulmonary diseases. He testified that the preclusions 
are permanent. (PX 1, p. 19). He testified that a diagnosis of chronic bronchitis by definition would indicate 
some impairment in the function of the lungs and airways. (PX 1, pp. 19-20). 
 
Dr. Istanbouly testified that in order to have pneumoconiosis, one must have, in addition to coal mine dust 
deposited in his lungs, a tissue reaction to it, and the tissue reaction can be called scarring or fibrosis. (PX 1, p. 
21). He testified that, by definition, if one has coal workers' pneumoconiosis, he necessarily has some 
impairment in the function of the lung at the site of the scarring, whether it can be measured by spirometry or 
not. (PX 1, pp. 21-23). 
 
Dr. Istanbouly testified that a person can have coal workers’ pneumoconiosis that is radiographically significant 
but not have shortness of breath, and a person can have radiographically significant coal workers’ 
26IWCC0133

 
5
pneumoconiosis and have normal pulmonary function testing, normal blood gases, and normal physical 
examination of the chest. He testified that coal workers’ pneumoconiosis is considered to be a progressive 
disease. He testified there is no cure for coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, and if a miner has coal workers’ 
pneumoconiosis and ends his exposure to coal mine dust, it can still progress. He testified that if a miner has 
coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, any further coal exposure would increase the progression of the disease. (PX 1, 
pp. 25-27). He testified that the progression of coal workers’ pneumoconiosis is usually gradual. (PX 1, pp. 27-
28).  
 
Dr. Istanbouly testified that the number of years required to develop pneumoconiosis varies from individual to 
individual, and that for some, it takes 40 years, and others it occurred in two years. He testified that he is 
familiar with the positions of the National Institute of Occupational Safety and Health and the Department of 
Labor that have been published in the Federal Register dated in the year 2000 concerning obstructive lung 
disease and coal mine dust, wherein they reference the fact that coal dust is half as much importance as cigarette 
smoke in causing emphysema. (PX 1, p. 32). 
 
Dr. Istanbouly testified that chronic bronchitis is one of the chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases, and a 
person can have chronic bronchitis and have normal pulmonary function testing, normal blood gas testing, and a 
normal physical examination of the chest. He testified that if a person has further exposure to coal mine dust 
after he has chronic bronchitis, it can make chronic bronchitis worse. (PX 1, pp. 34-35).  
 
He testified when a miner leaves a coal mine after 20 years or more, he will have coal mine dust that stays 
trapped in his lungs that he cannot get out and it will remain there for the rest of his life. In that case, the lung 
tissue that is next to the trapped coal mine dust will have exposure to coal mine dust for the rest of the miner's 
life, and that is one of the reasons it can progress. (PX 1, pp. 36-37). Dr. Istanbouly testified that if a miner has a 
positive chest x-ray and sufficient exposure, that is a sufficient basis for him to make a diagnosis of coal 
workers’ pneumoconiosis. He testified that a person can have coal workers’ pneumoconiosis on autopsy or 
biopsy and have a normal chest x-ray. He testified that at the location of the lesion, there is an impairment in the 
function of the lung tissue. (PX 1, pp. 37-38). He testified that anybody that has coal dust in his lung has 
pathological pneumoconiosis. (PX 1, pp. 39-41). 
 
Dr. Istanbouly testified that he saw Petitioner only one time at his attorney's request for a workup for his state 
black lung claim. He testified that he performs these types of examinations when he travels to Southern Illinois 
once a month. (PX 1, pp. 41-42). Dr. Istanbouly testified that Petitioner related a significant and continuing 
smoking history, and that such a history is known to be associated with cough, sputum, dyspnea on exertion, 
COPD, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and pulmonary fibrosis. He testified that Petitioner had a smoker's 
cough because it was most prominent in the morning. He testified that Petitioner said his cough was aggravated 
by strenuous activities and laughing but did not specify that it was aggravated by dust. Dr. Istanbouly testified 
Petitioner related to him exertional dyspnea. He testified that there are causes for exertional dyspnea other than 
respiratory disease, including heart disease and deconditioning. (PX 1, pp. 42-43). He testified that a person can 
have chronic cough that is multifactorial in etiology, and that was what Petitioner had because there is no 
inconsistency between smoker's cough and coal workers’ pneumoconiosis-related cough. He testified that there 
is no testing that is available that would apportion the amount of his cough that is due to one etiology versus the 
other. (PX 1, pp. 51-52). 
 
Dr. Istanbouly testified Petitioner told him he left the mine due to being laid off and that he specifically asked 
Petitioner if it had anything to do with health issues and Petitioner said it had nothing to do with health reasons. 
(PX 1, pp. 43-44). Dr. Istanbouly testified that he did not review any treatment records for Petitioner. He 
testified that on examination Petitioner's pulse ox was 96% which is within the normal range. Physical 
examination of his chest revealed no signs of respiratory disease, no crackles, rales, or wheeze. Petitioner's 
spirometry was within the normal range, and his FVC of 93% was not consistent or suggestive of restrictive 
26IWCC0133

 
6
defect and his FEV1 of 90% was also normal. (PX 1, pp. 44-46).  Dr. Istanbouly testified that he indicated in his 
report that the FEV1/FVC ratio was 71%, but that was not Petitioner's best effort. He testified Petitioner's best 
effort was 73 and his report should state 73%. (PX 1, p. 46). Dr. Istanbouly testified that Petitioner did not tell 
him he ever took any breathing medications. (PX 1, p. 47).  He testified that due to the fact of Petitioner’s 
continued smoking, he anticipates a decline in Petitioner's spirometry over time if he continues that habit. He 
testified that Petitioner’s lung function is expected to decline and he expects an increase in Petitioner's 
symptoms if he continues to smoke. He testified that smoking was injurious to Petitioner's health. (PX 1, p. 48).   
 
Dr. Istanbouly testified that he did not review any chest imaging of Petitioner. He testified that it is his 
preference in performing examinations of individuals for the presence of black lung that he has a chest x-ray of 
the individual to review, as it is more helpful. He testified that he had the report and B-reading of Dr. Smith for 
the November 25th of 2022 x-ray, and it is the only interpretation he has seen of chest imaging of Petitioner. 
(PX 1, pp. 48-49). Dr. Istanbouly testified that a person must be a susceptible host to develop coal workers’ 
pneumoconiosis and that not all miners do. (PX 1, p. 50).  
 
Dr. Henry K. Smith report 
 
Dr. Henry K. Smith interpreted Petitioner’s chest x-ray of November 25, 2022. He interpreted same as positive 
for simple coal workers’ pneumoconiosis with p/p opacities in all zones of profusion 1/0. Dr. Smith is a board-
certified radiologist and NIOSH B-reader. (PX 2, pp. 1-2).  
 
Dr. Cristopher Meyer Testimony 
 
Dr. Cristopher Meyer reviewed chest radiographs of Petitioner dated March 22, 2011, and November 25, 2022, 
and a CT from July 7, 2020. Dr. Meyer testified that the March 22, 2011, PA chest x-ray was quality 3. He 
testified it was overexposed but readable. He testified the lungs were clear and there were no findings of coal 
workers’ pneumoconiosis. (RX 1, pp. 41-42). Dr. Meyer testified that the November 25, 2022, x-ray showed 
some small opacities, of size s and size t, bilaterally in primarily the mid and upper long zones that were linear 
and irregular, with profusion of 1/0. He testified there were no large opacities, and some findings of lower 
cervical spine fusion. He testified that there were classifiable parenchymal abnormalities, not typical for coal 
workers’ pneumoconiosis, which is classically small and round. He testified the linear opacities seen are more 
typical of other causes of interstitial lung disease. He testified that based on his experience and studies linear 
opacities can be seen with significant tobacco use. (RX 1, p. 44). Dr. Meyer testified that he cannot recall one 
example where he saw only linear opacities and no round opacities in coal workers and stated such an 
occurrence would be likely related to Petitioner’s smoking history. (RX 1, pp. 46-47).  
 
Dr. Meyer testified that the July 7, 2020, CT revealed areas of peripheral ground glass opacity and some septal 
thickening. He testified he observed a calcified granuloma present in the right lower lobe. He testified there 
were no large opacities, and there was apical paraseptal emphysema. He testified he observed calcified right 
hilar lymph nodes and calcified granulomas in the spleen, which were evidence of sequalae of prior 
granulomatous disease. Dr. Meyer testified that the CT Petitioner received covered the entire lung and is better 
at detecting small nodules, and despite that, there were no centrilobular or perilymphatic nodules that are the 
classic manifestation of coal workers’ pneumoconiosis. (RX 1, pp. 49-50). He testified that peripheral ground 
glass septal thickening and paraseptal emphysema are characteristic of smoking-related interstitial lung disease. 
He testified that what he observed in Petitioner’s CT was smoking-related interstitial lung disease. Dr. Meyer 
testified that the calcified granuloma was separate from the interstitial lung disease and is a frequent finding for 
persons living in the Ohio or Mississippi River Valley due to a fungus, histoplasmosis. He testified the fungus 
was endemic in both river valleys. He testified that many people in the areas have been exposed and will be left 
with small areas of granulomas, which are little scars of walled-off infection. (RX 1, pp. 50-51). 
 
26IWCC0133

 
7
Dr. Meyer testified that, based on the CT scan, it is not possible to determine exactly how long the lung changes 
have been present. He testified that some findings, such as ground-glass opacities, fall within the spectrum of 
smoking-related interstitial lung disease and may even improve if the patient stops smoking. He testified that 
because these findings can be variable over time, the precise onset cannot be established. He testified that 
considering Petitioner’s 40-year smoking history, the timing and appearance of the abnormalities are consistent 
with smoking-related interstitial lung disease. (RX 1, pp. 53-54). Dr. Meyer testified that the CT scan and the 
chest x-ray from November 2022 were concordant. He testified that ground-glass are incredibly difficult to 
detect on a standard chest x-ray, so it is not surprising that they are more clearly visible on CT imaging. On the 
follow-up chest x-ray taken two years later, he rated the small opacities as a profusion of 1/0, which indicates 
changes that are barely perceptible. He testified that the CT findings were mild, and the degree of involvement 
seen on CT would reasonably correspond to a 1/0 profusion score on chest radiography. He testified that the s- 
and t-type opacities he observed are the smaller, irregular types of opacities typical with septal irregularity. Dr. 
Meyer testified that his findings concerning the July 7, 2020 CT scan were concordant with those of Dr. Becker. 
(RX 1, pp. 55-56). Dr. Meyer opined, within a reasonable degree of medical certainty, that the cause of the 
findings on Petitioner’s x-ray, other than the calcified granuloma, is smoking-related interstitial lung disease. 
(RX 1, pp. 111-112). 
 
Dr. Meyer testified that he did not review any medical of Petitioner other than the imaging studies themselves. 
He testified he generally prefers not to know anything about the individual, and he believes objectivity is 
hampered by having all the background historical information. He testified that because he is using chest 
radiographs as one of the objective measures of interstitial lung disease, he assumes that the individual has 
adequate exposure history to be screened, and he just wants to apply the epidemiologic approach that he learned 
in the B-reading syllabus and the course to give his best estimate of the presence or absence of opacities and the 
profusion of those. (RX 1, p. 48).  
 
Dr. Meyer has been board certified in radiology since 1992. (RX 1, p. 8). Dr. Meyer became a B-reader in 1999. 
Dr. Meyer testified that the B-reader course involves a structured training module, which includes a syllabus 
with case images, online resources provided by NIOSH, and an intensive training weekend course hosted by the 
American College of Radiology. Dr. Meyer is currently co-director of the ACR B-reader course and as a 
member of the ACR Pneumoconiosis Task Force participated in developing the new syllabus and test materials 
provided to NIOSH in 2017. (RX 1, pp. 33-34). 
 
Dr. Meyer testified that one of the most important parts of the B-reading training and examination is making the 
distinction between a film with profusion of 0/1 which is a normal examination from 1/0 which is an almost 
normal but slightly abnormal examination. Dr. Meyer testified that making the distinction between a film with 
1/0 profusion versus a 0/1 profusion is a critical component of the B-reader examination and is a point of 
emphasis in the B-reading course as well. (RX 1, p. 36).  
 
Dr. Meyer testified that the B-reader must first evaluate the quality of the film to describe any limitations of the 
x-ray. Dr. Meyer testified that the B-reader looks at the lungs to decide whether there are small nodular 
opacities and based on the size and appearance of the small opacities they are given a letter score.  He testified it 
is important for a B-reader to show the small opacities and their distribution. (RX 1, p. 24). Dr. Meyer testified 
that specific occupational lung diseases are described by specific opacity types. Coal workers’ pneumoconiosis 
is characteristically described by small round opacities. Diseases that cause pulmonary fibrosis, like asbestosis, 
are described by small linear opacities. (RX 1, p. 30). The distribution of the opacities is also described because 
different pneumoconioses are seen in different regions of the lung. Coal workers’ pneumoconiosis is typically 
an upper lung zone predominant process. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or asbestosis is a basilar or linear 
process. The last component of the interpretation is the extent of the lung involvement or so-called profusion. 
(RX 1, pp. 24-25).  Dr. Meyer testified that profusion is basically trying to define the concentration of the small 
opacities in the lung. (RX 1, pp. 31-32). Dr. Meyer testified that NIOSH provides standard ILO films for the 
26IWCC0133

 
8
interpreter to compare and grade x-rays. (RX 1, p. 65). He testified that as a B-reader, when one fills out the B-
reading form and he sees abnormalities consistent with coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, the reader is supposed to 
mark those on the form wherever they may occur. (RX 1, p. 83). 
 
Dr. Meyer testified that the gold standard for determining lung disease is the pathologic review of lung tissue 
rather than radiographic interpretation. (RX 1, p. 67). Dr. Meyer testified that when he was reading films two 
days a week, he read between 150 to 200 chest x-rays in a week and depending upon the busyness of the 
service, he read 50 to 70 chest CT scans. (RX 1, pp. 16-17). Dr. Meyer testified that per month he performs 
approximately 50 to 100 B-readings and reads approximately 10 to 20 CT scans for the purpose of determining 
the presence, absence, or severity of occupational lung disease. (RX 1, p. 86-87). 
 
Dr. Meyer testified that two equally qualified B-readers could look at a film and arrive at different conclusions. 
(RX 1, p. 69). He testified that one of the issues is making sure that the individual who is interpreting the 
examinations has ample experience reading them to be able to sort out what is the background variation in 
normal. He testified that people are as different on the outside as they are on the inside, and part of trying to 
figure out whether or not there is an additional abnormality in the lung is recognizing that large spectrum of 
normal, which is why someone like himself spends his entire career as a chest radiologist devoted to looking at 
chest radiographs day in and day out to establish that spectrum of normal. (RX 1, pp. 69-70). Dr. Meyer 
testified that CTs are the most sensitive exams which have the highest opportunity to identify abnormalities. 
(RX 1, p. 71). 
 
Dr. Meyer testified that all long-term coal miners are going to come out with some coal dust trapped in their 
lungs, however, the majority will not have changes in their lungs that qualify for coal workers' pneumoconiosis. 
He testified that the manifestations of pneumoconiosis are based on one's body's ability to clear that dust. Dr.

Dr. David Rosenberg Testimony 
 
Dr. David Rosenberg conducted a review of medical records and chest imaging regarding Petitioner at the 
request of Respondent’s counsel. (RX 3, p. 11). Dr. Rosenberg has been board certified in internal medicine 
since 1977. After graduating from medical school, he did a pulmonary fellowship at the National Institute of 
Health in Bethesda, Maryland. Dr. Rosenberg received his board certification in pulmonary disease in 1980. 
(RX 3, pp. 4-5). In 1995, he received his board certification in occupational medicine. (Respondent’s Exhibit 
No. 3, p. 5). Dr. Rosenberg has patients in his clinical practice he is treating who have black lung. (RX 3, p. 10).  
 
Dr. Rosenberg reviewed a chest x-ray for Petitioner dated November 25, 2022, from Harrisburg Medical 
Center. He noted that the film quality was 1. He noted it revealed s/t changes in the right mid and upper lung 
zones with a profusion rating of 1/0. (RX 3, p. 35). Dr. Rosenberg testified that for a proper reading of a chest 
x-ray for pneumoconiosis, the reader first assesses the quality of the film. He testified that he next evaluates 
whether there are any parenchymal changes. If they are present, he determines whether they are primary or 
secondary micronodular or linear changes. The reader next notes which of the lung zones are involved. The 
reader notes the profusion rating and whether there are any large opacities. (RX 3, p. 36).  Dr. Rosenberg 
testified that the reader then classifies any pleural abnormalities and notes on the B-reading form whether there 
are any other abnormalities. Dr. Rosenberg testified that the interpretation of the target film is done side-by-side 
with the standard ILO films and he uses the side-by-side comparison when making his interpretations. (RX 3, 
pp. 36-37). Dr. Rosenberg testified that the gold standard for determining coal workers’ pneumoconiosis is

pathologic review. He testified an individual could have a negative chest x-ray but be found to have coal 
workers’ pneumoconiosis pathologically. (RX 3, p. 69-71).  
 
Dr. Rosenberg also reviewed a chest CT dated July 7, 2020, from Memorial Medical Center and noted 
peripheral areas of ground-glass changes and some focal scarring. He noted mild emphysematous changes with 
granuloma formation and noted there was no micronodulariy related to past coal mine dust exposure. (RX 3, p.

Dr. Rosenberg is familiar with the AMA Guides to the Evaluation of Permanent Impairment, Sixth Edition, 
Chapter 5, The Pulmonary System. He testified that chest imaging under the Guides is not a factor, let alone a 
key factor, in the assessment of pulmonary impairment. He testified that he agrees with the Guides that the 
correlation of chest x-ray interpretation and physiologic measurement is poor. (RX 3, pp. 25-26). Dr. Rosenberg 
testified that cough is not an objective determinant of pulmonary impairment. To determine whether a person 
suffers from pulmonary impairment one would want, if available, spirometry, diffusion capacity, lung volumes, 
and some measure of gas exchange. He testified that a history of coal dust exposure and changes in pulmonary 
function are not enough to make a diagnosis of coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, but one needs objective 
information such as imaging that shows changes in the lung or pathologic evidence of disease. (RX 3, p. 23-25). 
Dr. Rosenberg testified that an individual needs to be a susceptible host to develop coal workers’ 
pneumoconiosis. He testified that only a minority of coal miners develop same. Dr. Rosenberg testified that the 
intensity or the duration of exposure for the individual is not important if the individual is not a susceptible host. 
He testified that those individuals are not going to develop the disease. (RX 3, pp. 26-27). 
 
Dr. Rosenberg testified that the results from the pulmonary function testing performed on Petitioner at Stat-Care 
on April 24, 2023 was normal. He testified there was no evidence of obstruction or restriction. Dr. Rosenberg 
testified that Petitioner’s diffusion capacity was reduced and he attributed it to his smoking. He testified that it 
is known that smoking both directly and artificially can lower the diffusion capacity measurement. He testified 
that diffusion capacity testing is an indirect measurement of gas exchange. Diffusion capacity testing uses 
carbon monoxide to measure gas exchange, and a smoker likely has elevated carbon monoxide levels in the 
bloodstream prior to taking the test. According to the records, Petitioner was a long-time smoker, recorded at 
some points as two packs a day, and such smoking could markedly increase carbon monoxide in his 
bloodstream. Dr. Rosenberg testified that even if a smoker abstains for six hours prior to the test, he will still be 
left with a high level because it's only going down by half in four to six hours.  (RX 3, pp. 30-32). Dr. 
Rosenberg testified that if he applied Table 5-4 of the Guides to pulmonary function testing performed on 
Petitioner, he would fall into class 0 impairment.  He testified that the recommended standard document 
published by NIOSH outlines that any reduction in diffusion capacity in relationship to coal dust exposure is 
minimal. (RX 3, p. 33). Dr. Rosenberg testified that it is unlikely for simple pneumoconiosis to progress once 
the exposure ceases. Dr. Rosenberg agrees with the American Thoracic Society that an older worker with a mild 
pneumoconiosis may be at low risk for working in the mine at currently permissible dust levels until he reaches 
retirement age. (RX 3, p. 38).

Rosenberg testified that Petitioner had episodes of acute bronchitis and sinusitis in the past, but more recent 
treatment records do not describe chronic respiratory symptomatology of coughing, congestion, or shortness of

Petitioner was examined once by Dr. Suhail Istanbouly, who diagnosed simple coal workers’ pneumoconiosis 
caused by coal dust exposure and chronic bronchitis caused by exposure to both coal dust and smoking. His 
opinion, however, relied heavily on Dr. Henry Smith’s B-reading of a November 25, 2022, chest x-ray. Dr. 
Istanbouly did not personally review any imaging studies, acknowledged that spirometry and oxygen saturation 
were normal, and found no abnormal lung findings on physical examination.

Dr. Smith, a B-reader, interpreted the November 25, 2022, chest x-ray as positive for simple pneumoconiosis 
with profusion 1/0. Dr. Smith did not testify, and his interpretation is countered by the testimony of two other 
highly credentialed B-readers who personally reviewed the same and additional imaging studies. 
 
Dr. Cristopher Meyer, a board-certified radiologist and long-time B-reader, reviewed the 2011 and 2022 chest 
radiographs as well as a 2020 CT scan. He testified that the 2011 x-ray was negative for pneumoconiosis, and 
the 2022 film showed irregular linear opacities consistent with smoking-related interstitial lung disease rather 
than coal workers’ pneumoconiosis. He noted apical emphysema and ground-glass changes on CT, findings 
classic for smoking-related lung disease consistent with Petitioner’s extensive tobacco history. Dr. Meyer 
concluded, within a reasonable degree of medical certainty, that the radiological abnormalities were attributable 
to smoking, not coal dust exposure. 
 
Dr. David Rosenberg, a board-certified pulmonologist, occupational medicine specialist, and B-reader, 
reviewed the same 2022 chest x-ray and 2020 CT. He acknowledged the presence of s/t opacities but concluded 
the findings, including scarring and ground-glass changes, were consistent with smoking-related interstitial lung 
disease rather than pneumoconiosis. He emphasized that diagnosis of pneumoconiosis must be supported by 
imaging or pathology, not merely symptoms or normal spirometry. Pulmonary function testing performed in 
2023 revealed no obstruction or restriction, and Dr. Rosenberg credibly attributed the reduced diffusion capacity 
to ongoing tobacco use. He opined that Petitioner does not have coal workers’ pneumoconiosis or any form of 
lung disease related to his past coal mine dust exposure. 
 
Both Dr. Rosenberg and Dr. Istanbouly agree that any diagnosis of coal workers’ pneumoconiosis must rest on 
objective imaging or pathology. There is no biopsy or autopsy evidence in this record. Thus, the issue turns on 
the credibility of the imaging interpretations. Dr. Istanbouly did not review the imaging himself and relied 
solely on Dr. Smith’s B-reading, despite acknowledging it was his preference to personally review the films. In 
contrast, Dr. Meyer and Dr. Rosenberg personally reviewed multiple studies and gave consistent, well-
supported explanations why the observed abnormalities are characteristic of smoking-related interstitial lung 
disease, not occupational pneumoconiosis. The Arbitrator finds their testimony is more persuasive. 
 
Finally, Petitioner’s medical history does not support his claim. He has severe peripheral vascular disease 
requiring bypass surgery, diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia, all unrelated to occupational exposures. 
Repeated treatment records from Springfield Clinic and Springfield Memorial consistently document clear 
lungs, normal breath sounds, and no persistent pulmonary abnormalities. Pulmonary function testing in 2023 
showed normal spirometry, with reduced diffusion capacity credibly explained by smoking. Despite Petitioner’s 
testimony of exertional limitations and cough, his recent medical records frequently note denials of shortness of 
breath, cough, or wheeze, and confirm clear lung sounds. 
 
Accordingly, Petitioner has failed to prove that he suffers from coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, chronic 
bronchitis, or any other occupational lung disease causally related to his coal mine employment.  
 
Issue (O): Whether Petitioner proved timely disablement pursuant to Section 1(e) and (f) of the 
Occupational Diseases Act? 
 
The Arbitrator concludes that Petitioner failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that he suffered a 
timely disablement as described in Sections 1(e) and (f) of the Occupational Diseases Act. In support of this 
conclusion, the Arbitrator notes the following:

17
Section 1(e) of the Occupational Diseases Act states as follows: 
“Disablement” means an impairment or partial impairment, temporary or permanent, in the 
function of the body or any of the members of the body, or the event of becoming disabled 
from earning full wages at the work in which the employee was engaged when last exposed 
to the hazards of the occupational disease by the employer from whom he or she claims 
compensation, or equal wages in other suitable employment; and “disability” means the 
state of being so incapacitated. 820 ILCS 310/1(e). 
Section 1(f) of the Act provides that said disablement must be present within two years after the last date of 
exposure to the hazards of an occupational disease. 820 ILCS 310/1(f). Petitioner failed to prove either an 
impairment or partial impairment or the event of becoming disabled from earning full wages as a coal miner or 
in other suitable employment.  
 
Petitioner testified that he left the mine due to a layoff along with other miners. Petitioner related to Dr. 
Istanbouly that he did not leave his coal mine employment because of respiratory impairment or inability to 
perform his job duties. He has not worked since his layoff, but the medical evidence does not establish that this 
was due to pulmonary disease. In fact, the medical records reflect largely normal pulmonary function testing, 
repeated denials of shortness of breath to treating providers, and clear lung examinations in the years following 
his departure from mining. There is no medical evidence indicating any physician has restricted Petitioner from 
working due to a respiratory condition. 
 
Dr. Rosenberg testified that Petitioner’s April 2023 pulmonary function testing revealed no obstruction or 
restriction, and that the only abnormality was a reduced diffusion capacity, which he credibly attributed to long-
term smoking and elevated carbon monoxide levels from ongoing tobacco use. He further testified that if Table 
5-4 of the Guides is applied, Petitioner would fall into class 0 impairment. There is no evidence in the record 
disputing the class 0 impairment rating. Dr. Rosenberg emphasized that cough is not an objective determinant of 
pulmonary impairment and that chest imaging is not a key factor under the Guides to determine impairment. Dr. 
Rosenberg further explained that recent cigarette smoking can artificially lower DLCO results, and the 
technician administering Petitioner’s April 2023 testing documented a strong odor of cigarette smoke upon his 
arrival, supporting Rosenberg’s conclusion that the reduced diffusion capacity was attributable to ongoing 
tobacco use rather than occupational lung disease. 
 
Dr. Istanbouly’s testimony that conditions such as reduced DLCO, chronic bronchitis, or coal workers’ 
pneumoconiosis would “by definition” involve some level of pulmonary impairment does not satisfy the legal 
standard for proving impairment. The Occupational Diseases Act and the AMA Guides require objective 
evidence of functional limitation, such as measurable abnormalities on pulmonary function testing, diffusion 
capacity, or gas exchange studies. Simply stating that a diagnosis presumes some impairment is not equivalent 
to demonstrating an actual loss of lung function. In this case, Petitioner’s spirometry was normal, oxygen 
saturation was within normal range, and repeated physical examinations documented clear lung sounds. 
Therefore, Dr. Istanbouly’s “by definition” assertions describe theoretical consequences of disease, but they do 
not establish that Petitioner has a measurable or disabling pulmonary impairment as required by law. The 
diagnosis of an occupational disease does not equate to a finding of disablement. Hicks v. Industrial 
Commission, 251 Ill. App. 3d 320 (5th Dist. 1993); Meracle v. The American Coal Company, 24 IWCC 0616. 
 
Given the Arbitrator’s findings on disease, causation, and disablement, all other issues are rendered moot. 
 
Petitioner’s claim for benefits under the Act is denied.
